paragraphs.heading: Ions in a cloud of electrons
paragraphs.text: Metallic bonding is a type of chemical bonding. It comes from the electrostatic pull between positively charged metal ions and a cloud of delocalized conduction electrons, which are shared freely across the structure of ions. Metal atoms give up their valence electrons to one large delocalized orbital, leaving the nucleus and its inner electrons behind as positive ions. The negative charge of that orbital then holds the ions together in a crystal lattice.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: One way to picture it is free electrons shared among a framework of positive ions, a more spread-out version of covalent bonding. This kind of bonding explains many physical properties of metals: strength, ductility, how they conduct heat and electricity, opacity and lustre. It is mostly non-polar, because the atoms taking part, even in alloys, differ little or not at all in electronegativity.

paragraphs.heading: From an ocean of electrons to models
paragraphs.text: Electrochemistry showed that metals generally dissolve as positively charged ions. From this grew a picture of a metal as positive ions bound by an ocean of negative electrons. Quantum mechanics later gave the picture a formal shape in the free electron model and its extension, the nearly free electron model. In both, the electrons behave like a gas moving through the solid.

paragraphs.heading: Right answers, wrong idea
paragraphs.text: The metallurgist Hume-Rothery used the nearly free electron model to explain why alloys of some compositions form and others do not. He pictured adding electrons to inflate a spherical balloon, the Fermi surface, inside a series of boxes, and asked when a given box would fill. The idea predicted quite a few alloy compositions that were observed later. But once cyclotron resonance could measure the balloon's shape, it turned out not to be spherical, except perhaps in caesium. A model can make a run of correct predictions and still rest on wrong assumptions.

paragraphs.heading: Newer pictures
paragraphs.text: Researchers went on to build quantum mechanical models such as band structure calculations and density functional theory. Band structure became a major focus in studying metals and, even more, semiconductors. Yet it is a one-electron approximation: each electron is treated as if all the others formed an even background. The free electron picture still dominates introductory courses on metallurgy.

paragraphs.heading: What makes it work
paragraphs.text: Two things together give rise to metallic bonding: electrons are delocalized, and there are far more delocalized energy states available than there are delocalized electrons. That second feature could be called electron deficiency. A metal crystal can even be seen as a single molecule, with its conduction electrons spread through all three dimensions. So inside a metal one generally cannot tell separate molecules apart, which makes the bonding neither within nor between molecules.

paragraphs.heading: Not one single bond
paragraphs.text: Metallic bonding exists only in condensed matter, whether a crystalline solid or a liquid. Metal vapours are different: they are often single atoms, as with mercury, or sometimes molecules like Na₂ held by a more ordinary covalent bond. That is why it is not correct to speak of one single metallic bond.
